note: Dead once as shades, and so wasted by hunger that they look as if they had died again. These are the gluttons of the sixth terrace.

context: Dante is still walking beside him, as in Canto 23. Forese will point out his fellow penitents, foretell the death of his own brother, and then run on.
Dante has just pointed him out to Forese. Statius is free to go straight up to Heaven, and Dante guesses that he is lingering for the pleasure of Virgil's company.

note: Heaven, called by the name of the mountain where the Greek gods lived.
More than allowed: it is needed. Starvation has wiped out every likeness, so no one here could be known by his face.
Bonagiunta Orbicciani, a notary and poet of Lucca who died in the 1290s. He wrote love poems in the older manner that Dante's generation set out to replace. He will speak for that older school.
A city in Tuscany, west of Florence.

quote: held the Holy Church in his embrace
note: A pope: the Church is his bride. This is Martin IV, pope from 1281 to 1285, a Frenchman.
A city on the Loire in France. Martin was not born there, but he had been treasurer of its cathedral.
Lake Bolsena, north of Rome, was famous for its eels. Early commentators say Pope Martin had them drowned in white wine and then roasted, and that he died of eating too many.
A prized Italian white wine.
In lower Hell the damned often try to hide who they are. Here the souls are glad to be named: a living man who knows them can ask for prayers on their behalf.

A Tuscan nobleman of the Ubaldini family, named for his castle of La Pila in the hills north of Florence. He was the brother of the Cardinal in Inferno 10 and the father of Archbishop Ruggieri, whose skull Count Ugolino gnaws in Inferno 33.

Not Pope Boniface VIII. This is Bonifazio dei Fieschi, of a great Genoese family, archbishop of Ravenna from 1274 to 1295. Dante may be hinting that he fed a crowd of hangers-on rather than a flock of souls.
Dante's word is "rook", like the chess piece. The staff of the archbishops of Ravenna is said to have ended in a piece of that shape, not in the usual curved crook.

A nobleman of Forlì, a town in Romagna, known as a great drinker. Early commentators tell this story: told that people said he did nothing but drink, he answered, "Why don't they say that I am always thirsty?"
Bonagiunta, named a few lines earlier.
Most likely a woman's name, and the woman of the prophecy that follows. Who she was is not known for certain.
His mouth, parched and starved, where the penance of this terrace is felt.

quote: does not yet wear the veil
note: The head covering of a married woman. In 1300 she is still a girl. Dante stayed in Lucca for a time during his exile, and a lady there was evidently kind to him. Nothing in the text suggests a love affair.
Dante himself, for one. In Inferno 21 a devil says that everyone in Lucca takes bribes.
Dante's Italian says simply "the new rhymes".

"Donne ch'avete intelletto d'amore", the first long poem in Dante's Vita Nuova, the little book about his love for Beatrice. There he says that with this poem he found a new subject: simply to praise her, and ask for nothing in return.

Dante's account of his own poetry, and one of the most quoted passages in the poem. He claims no skill. Love breathes in him and dictates, and he takes down what he hears, like a scribe. "Inspires" keeps its first sense in the Italian: breathes into.
Dante's word is "the knot": what tied the older poets and kept them from reaching the new manner.

Giacomo da Lentini, a court official of the emperor Frederick II in Sicily in the first half of the 13th century. He was the leading poet of the Sicilian school, the first poets of love in Italian, and is usually credited with inventing the sonnet.
Guittone d'Arezzo, who died in 1294, the most admired Tuscan poet of the generation before Dante. Dante thought his verse clumsy and overrated, and says so again in Canto 26.

In Italian, dolce stil novo. Historians of literature took the phrase from this line as the name for a whole school: Guido Guinizzelli of Bologna, then Guido Cavalcanti, Dante and their friends in Florence. Whether Dante meant a school or only his own poetry is debated.
Love. Bonagiunta admits that the older poets wrote from convention, not from what love told them.

A hard pair of lines in the Italian, and scholars read them in several ways. The likeliest sense: this is the whole difference between the two styles, and anyone who looks for another will not find it.
Cranes, flying south to Egypt for the winter.
They are light in body from hunger, and light in will because they are eager to get on with their penance.

quote: When will I see you again?
note: A gentle way of asking a living man when he expects to die.
However soon he dies, he will have wished to be back on this shore sooner. He is sick of the world, and above all of his city.

quote: The place where I was born to live
context: In the spring of 1300 the quarrel between the White and Black parties was about to break into open violence. Within two years Dante was banished.

note: Corso Donati, Forese's own brother, leader of the Black party in Florence, whose seizure of the city in 1301 led to Dante's exile. He is never named in the poem. Of the three Donati, Forese is in Purgatory, Piccarda is in Heaven, and Corso is bound for Hell.

In 1308 Corso was accused of plotting to make himself lord of Florence. He fled and was caught. The chroniclers say he fell or threw himself from his horse and was killed by his guards. Dante turns this into a horse dragging him at its tail, faster and faster, straight to Hell.
Hell, where no sin can ever be undone.
The heavens, which turn around the earth and measure time. Not many years will pass: eight, as it turned out.
Virgil and Statius, great commanders in the world of poetry. The image follows from the knight in the simile just before.
The second tree of the terrace. The first, in Canto 22, called out examples of temperance. This one will call out examples of gluttony and what came of it.
The souls reach up and beg for fruit like children teased by an adult who holds a treat out of reach. Then they walk on, cured for the moment of the wish.

context: The first sin was an act of eating. The forbidden tree stands in the Garden of Eden at the top of the mountain (Canto 32), and this tree grew from a cutting of it.

note: The Centaurs, half man and half horse, hence their "double chests". In myth they were born when Ixion made love to a cloud shaped like the goddess Juno.

The hero of Athens. Ovid tells the story in the Metamorphoses. Invited to a wedding among the Lapiths, a people of Thessaly, the Centaurs got drunk and tried to carry off the bride and the other women. Theseus and the Lapiths fought them, and many Centaurs were killed.

A leader of Israel in the Book of Judges (chapter 7). On his way to fight the Midianites, God told him to watch his men drink at a stream. Those who went down on their knees to drink were sent home. He kept only the three hundred who lapped water from their hands, and won with them.
The Midianites, a desert people who were raiding Israel.
Each terrace ends with examples of its sin punished, as it began with examples of the opposite virtue. One example is from classical myth and one from the Bible, as usual.
The angel of the sixth terrace, glowing like metal in a furnace. It guards the stair to the seventh and last terrace.
The angel's wing brushes away the sixth of the seven P's cut there at the gate (Canto 9). Only one is left, the mark of lust.
The food of the gods in classical myth, known for its fragrance. After a terrace of hunger, the air itself smells of a heavenly meal.

The second half of the Beatitude begun in Canto 22: "Blessed are they who hunger and thirst after justice" (Matthew 5:6). There the angel spoke of thirst. Here the angel speaks of hunger, and reshapes the verse: blessed are those who hunger only as much as is right.
